Paris, October 1853.

From the notebook of François Arago, astronomer, Perpetual Secretary of the Academy of Sciences.

The weather this week has been fair, and I have been able to resume the measurements postponed since the spring. This morning I reviewed the accounts of the Observatory and signed the order for the new clock regulator. There is a letter from Leverrier still to answer, and the proofs of the memoir on terrestrial magnetism are late from the printer. Yesterday I said to my assistant:

“Young man, do you know what I like about our work?

“You ask why I like our work?”

“Yes, why I like it so much?

“I do not know.”

“Well, it is because we measure the sky. The sky!

“The sky?”

“The sky! The heavens!

“Oh.”

“The heavens! And how far

are the heavens?”

“Far?”

“Far? Oh, yes, they are very far. The sky is incomprehensible. It is not even the sky, it is infinity. That is what I like about our work: we measure infinity.

“I don’t understand.”

“It is a game we play, young man. We play at measuring the heavens.

are they away from us?

“I don’t know.”

“Well, it is at least a hundred thousand leagues, isn’t it?”

“Yes, at least a hundred thousand leagues.”

“And it is all there in front of us.”

“It is all there in front of us.”

“All that matter, all those stars, all those systems, all those nebulae,

away they are, how far away they are!

“Yes, they are far away.”

“And we measure them, we measure them, and we measure them!

“We measure them?”

“Yes, we measure them with our telescopes, with our instruments, with our own eyes!

“With our eyes?”

“Yes, with our own eyes!

“With our eyes, yes.”

I have lost the names of certain friends, and I do not remember all my enemies.
